processing: Black tea brewed without milk, finished with lemon or lime; some versions add ground cardamom and cinnamon, mint or basil, or saffron.
harvest_season: Not relevant: it is a prepared drink, usually from everyday black tea.
appearance_dry: Not sold as a distinct leaf; recipes often start from granular or dust black tea, such as Assam CTC.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden to amber, brightened by citrus.
appearance_wet: Not applicable: it is served strained.
taste_profile: Sweet and sour with a slight spice, citrus lifting a light black-tea base and no milk to soften it.

brewing.notes: Simmer any whole spices first, brew the tea briefly, sweeten, then add citrus off the heat. Strain into small glasses. Keep it light: amber, not dark.

vintage_note: Not sold by harvest or year: it is poured fresh in homes, restaurants and tea stalls. Any black tea used is simply an everyday current one.
description:
Sulaimani is the milk-free tea of Kerala's Malabar coast: amber, citrusy and lightly spiced, usually poured in small glasses. It is the tea that follows a heavy meal such as biryani, valued locally as a digestive.

It is brewed light and served with lemon or lime. Recipes split on the rest: some stay plain, others bring in cardamom and cinnamon, mint or basil, and sometimes saffron. The sweetener varies too, from sugar to jaggery.

The balance is the challenge. Over-steeping makes a tannic cup that citrus turns harsh, so keep the tea light. Add the citrus last, then taste before sweetening further.

There is no special product to buy; a plain black tea will do. Try it in Kozhikode if you can, and after a real biryani if not.
history:
Its origins rest on folklore. The usual account links it to Arab traders on the Malabar coast and a date-and-pepper drink called ghava; local spices were added, sugar replaced dates, and tea came later. None of this is firmly established.

The name took shape in Malabar and is commonly tied to the Arabic Sulaiman, 'man of peace'. In the Mappila Muslim community it is simmered in large vats and appears on wedding menus. It has since travelled to the UAE, and a Kerala tea chain, Club Sulaimani, took its name.
